title: Environmentally-controlled Microtensile Testing of Mechanically-adaptive Polymer Nanocomposites for ex vivo Characterization
protocol: Prepare PVAc-NC film with a thickness between 25 and 100 μm using solution casting and compression techniques.
Heat the film on a hot plate at 70 °C for two minutes to adhere it to a silicon wafer.
Laser-micromachine the film using CO2 direct-write laser parameters set to 1.0% power, 4.0% speed, and 1,000 pulses per inch.
Pattern setup samples into dogbone-shaped structures with lateral pad dimensions of 1.5 x 1.5 mm² and lateral beam dimensions of 300 x 3,000 μm².
Pattern implant samples for ex vivo experiments into beams measuring 300 μm x 6 mm, maintaining a thickness consistent with the film throughout.
Carefully release samples from the wafer using a razor blade and tweezers.
Prepare custom-machined acrylic holders for each implant sample.
Place cyanoacrylate gel-based adhesive on the centerline of the holder.
Adhere a 1.5 mm length of the implant sample to the holder, overlapping the marked centerline.
Ensure that the adhesive remains only along the 1.5 mm length of PVAc-NC.
Remove moisture from all samples by placing them in a desiccator for at least 24 hours.
Measure the length, width, and thickness dimensions of the samples using an optical microscope.
Load a dry setup sample into the microtensile tester, clamping between mobile grips first, then fixed grips.
Mount an air brush with a water-filled reservoir into a fixed position.
Connect the air brush to an air compressor via plastic tubing.
Turn on the air compressor.
Begin cyclic microtensile testing procedure.
Apply tensile strain (positive strain) to the sample.
Apply compressive strain (negative strain) to the sample.
Monitor stress-strain plot for linear elastic region behavior.
Limit applied strain to less than 2% for PVAc-NC samples.
Control strain rate while measuring required force.
Alternatively, control applied force while measuring resultant strain.
Gradually increase flow from air brush nozzle.
Monitor slope of stress-strain plot as a function of flow amount.
Determine maximum flow that does not cause >10% reduction in Young's modulus over 60 seconds.
Establish humidity conditions to prevent wetting and sample drying.
Measure temperature near the sample.
Set up thermocouple with digital readout for precise measurement.
Operate airbrush during temperature measurement procedure.
Adjust radiant heat source intensity and distance.
Maintain sample temperature at 37 °C to match physiological conditions.
Immerse setup samples in phosphate buffered saline for at least 30 minutes.
Load a PBS-saturated sample into the microtensile tester and begin cyclic testing with the air brush off.
Load a second PBS-saturated sample into the microtensile tester and begin cyclic testing with the air brush on.
Attach implant sample to a micromanipulator clamp and position orthogonal to the cortical tissue.
Keep tissue moist with saline prior to insertion.
Lower the polymer sample into the cortex using micromanipulator hand controls.
Leave the sample in cortical tissue until the target implant time, generally between 1 and 30 minutes.
Dab the tissue every 5 minutes using a saline-soaked cotton swab for time points over 5 minutes.
Set the drive rod of the microtensile tester to the zero-displacement position at 3.0 mm from the stationary sample clamp.
Adjust the air brush nozzle to the appropriate flow setting.
Set the radiant heat source to the intensity determined in Step 2.4.
Raise the probe out of the cortex using the micromanipulator hand controls at the end of the specified implant time.
Remove the sample carefully from the micromanipulator clamp immediately after raising the probe.
Load the sample into the microtensile tester as described in more detail in Step 5.2.
Load the sample between the two sets of microtensile tester clamps.
Place the implant sample assembly on the mobile grip, sample side down.
Ensure that the sample is mounted to the center of each clamp.
Adjust the distance between the clamps to 3.0 mm.
Place the end of the probe into the fixed clamp.
Activate the motor in the tensile direction at a constant rate of 10 μm/sec.
Measure and record the elongation of the sample using a displacement indicator.
Record the associated force required to strain the sample using a load cell.
Halt the microtensile test upon mechanical failure of the sample or when the end of the drive rod range is reached.
Repeat microtensile testing for each sample and/or each set of conditions.
Convert raw elongation data to engineering strain by dividing the distance of elongation by the initial gauge length.
Convert raw force data to engineering stress on the sample by dividing the force by the transverse cross-sectional area.
Plot the stress (σ[t]) vs. strain (ε[t]) curve for each sample using a computer program, such as Microsoft Excel.
Isolate the linear elastic portion of the plot and use software-based curve fitting tools to find the best fit line to this portion.
The slope of the best fit line corresponds to the Young's modulus of the sample.
Ensure the isolated portion of the plot includes at least 10 stress-strain points.
Take the isolated portion from where the slope is greatest.
Determine Young's modulus for each cycle in cyclic tests.
Plot the Young's modulus of each cycle versus time.
Measure the Young's modulus for each implant sample according to the described procedure.
Plot the Young's modulus versus implant time.
